subtopic_detail: Recognising a vascular birthmark in a location that threatens function
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 4 month old girl whose mother has brought her because of a lump on her eyelid. It appeared as a faint pink patch at about three weeks of age and has grown steadily since.

The lesion is a bright red raised swelling 25 mm across on the right upper eyelid that extends over the lid margin and pushes the lid down so that it covers the upper half of the pupil. It is soft, compressible and not tender, and there is no ulceration or bleeding. She is otherwise well, feeding and growing along the 50th centile, and has no other skin lesions.

data_table.Examination: Bright red compressible 25 mm lesion on the right upper eyelid overlying the lid margin and obscuring the upper half of the pupil, no ulceration, single lesion on full skin examination
data_table.Growth: Weight and length tracking along the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer urgently to ophthalmology and paediatrics for propranolol
options.rationale: A lesion obstructing the visual axis is a high risk infantile haemangioma that causes deprivation amblyopia within weeks, so it needs urgent specialist assessment and systemic propranolol after a cardiovascular check (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile Haemangioma).

options.text: Reassure the parents and review the lesion at twelve months of age
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is correct for most infantile haemangiomas because they involute, but involution begins around 12 months and by then irreversible amblyopia will have developed (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile Haemangioma).

options.text: Apply topical timolol maleate gel twice daily and review monthly
options.rationale: Topical beta blocker is effective for small superficial lesions of a few millimetres, and it penetrates too poorly to control a 25 mm periocular lesion (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile Haemangioma).

options.text: Refer for pulsed dye laser treatment at the next available list
options.rationale: Pulsed dye laser is used for residual telangiectasia after involution or for ulcerated lesions, and it does not control the deep proliferative component causing the obstruction (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile Haemangioma).

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the orbit before treatment
options.rationale: Imaging is reserved for segmental facial lesions raising the possibility of an associated syndrome or for suspected deep orbital extension, and arranging it first would delay sight saving treatment (Source: RCH CPG: Infantile Haemangioma).

explanation.summary: Infantile haemangiomas appear in the first weeks of life, proliferate rapidly until about five months, then involute slowly over years, and the great majority need no treatment at all. Treatment is reserved for lesions that threaten function, ulcerate, or will leave significant disfigurement, and the periocular site is the classic functional threat because occlusion of the visual axis for even a few weeks in infancy produces deprivation amblyopia. Astigmatism from pressure on the globe is a second mechanism of visual loss that persists even after the lesion shrinks, so ophthalmology follow up continues after treatment. Oral propranolol has replaced systemic corticosteroids and typically produces visible softening and colour change within days, with a pretreatment assessment for heart rate, blood pressure and any history suggesting airway or cardiac disease.
key_points: Proliferation peaks by about five months, before spontaneous involution begins
Periocular lesions cause deprivation amblyopia and astigmatism
Oral propranolol is first line for function threatening lesions
Topical timolol is limited to small superficial lesions
Five or more cutaneous haemangiomas prompts liver ultrasound
explanation.pearls: Five or more cutaneous infantile haemangiomas warrants abdominal ultrasound for hepatic haemangiomas, which can cause high output cardiac failure and consumptive hypothyroidism even when the skin lesions themselves are trivial.

subtopic_detail: Investigation after biochemistry confirms a central cause of early puberty
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a girl of 5 years and 6 months whose mother noticed breast development four months ago. Her height has crossed from the 50th to the 90th centile over the past year and her mother has noticed an adult body odour.

She has breast development to Tanner stage 3 and sparse pubic hair. She has no headache, no vomiting and no visual symptoms, and there are no cafe au lait macules on full skin examination and no history of unexplained laughing episodes. Her fundi are normal and her visual fields are full to confrontation.

data_table.Investigations: Luteinising hormone 4.2 IU/L after gonadotrophin releasing hormone stimulation indicating a pubertal response, oestradiol raised for age, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Bone age 9 years and 6 months against a chronological age of 5 years and 6 months, pelvic ultrasound shows an enlarged uterus with an endometrial stripe

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Arrange a pelvic ultrasound and repeat the bone age in six months
options.rationale: The pelvic ultrasound has already been done and repeating a bone age adds nothing when the diagnosis is biochemically established and the priority is to find the cause (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty).

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and pituitary
options.rationale: A pubertal luteinising hormone response to stimulation confirms a central cause, and every girl under 6 years with central precocious puberty needs brain imaging because the likelihood of an intracranial lesion is highest in this age group (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty).

options.text: Measure adrenal androgens and image the adrenal glands with CT
options.rationale: Adrenal investigation is for virilisation with a suppressed luteinising hormone response, and the near pair distinction is that a peripheral cause suppresses gonadotrophins while a central cause raises them (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty).

options.text: Commence a gonadotrophin releasing hormone analogue immediately
options.rationale: Treatment to halt puberty and preserve adult height is appropriate but is not an investigation, and starting it without imaging risks missing a hypothalamic lesion (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty).

options.text: Reassure the family and repeat the growth measurements in a year
options.rationale: Isolated premature thelarche without growth acceleration or bone age advance can be observed, and this girl has both a markedly advanced bone age and an oestrogenised uterus (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious Puberty).

explanation.summary: Precocious puberty means secondary sexual characteristics before 8 years of age in girls and 9 years in boys, and the first branch point is whether the cause is central, meaning early activation of the hypothalamic pituitary gonadal axis, or peripheral, meaning autonomous sex steroid production. A stimulated luteinising hormone response separates them, since central causes give a pubertal rise while peripheral causes suppress gonadotrophins through negative feedback. Central precocious puberty is idiopathic in the majority of girls but the proportion with an intracranial lesion rises sharply as the age at onset falls, which is why imaging is mandatory under 6 years and considered between 6 and 8 years. In boys the calculus is reversed, with a much higher rate of underlying pathology at any age, so imaging is arranged for all of them. Treatment with a gonadotrophin releasing hormone analogue aims to preserve adult height and to allow psychosocial development to match chronological age.
key_points: A pubertal luteinising hormone response to stimulation indicates a central cause
Peripheral causes suppress gonadotrophins through negative feedback
Brain imaging is mandatory for central precocious puberty in girls under 6 years
All boys with central precocious puberty need brain imaging
Bone age advance and an oestrogenised uterus separate this from premature thelarche
explanation.pearls: A hypothalamic hamartoma is the commonest intracranial cause of central precocious puberty and may be signalled by gelastic seizures, which parents describe as unexplained bursts of laughing rather than as seizures, so ask about them directly.

subtopic_detail: Vaccinating a child whose food allergy is widely but wrongly assumed to be a contraindication
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing an 11 month old boy who is due his scheduled vaccines including measles mumps rubella, and whose mother also wants this season's influenza vaccine given.

At seven months of age he developed widespread hives, vomiting and wheeze within 15 minutes of one mouthful of scrambled egg and was given intramuscular adrenaline in the emergency department. He has avoided egg since. He has no asthma and has had no previous vaccine reaction, and he is well and afebrile today.

data_table.Examination: Well child with clear chest, no rash and no fever
data_table.Immunisation history: Up to date on the National Immunisation Program schedule with no previous adverse events following immunisation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach today?

options.text: Refer to a specialist allergy clinic for vaccination in hospital
options.rationale: Hospital vaccination is reserved for a previous anaphylaxis to a vaccine or to a vaccine component such as gelatin, not for food allergy to egg (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook; ASCIA).

options.text: Give the measles mumps rubella vaccine but omit the influenza one
options.rationale: Modern influenza vaccines contain ovalbumin below 1 microgram per dose and are given routinely to children with egg anaphylaxis, so omitting it withholds protection without reason (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook).

options.text: Give both vaccines today with the standard 15 minute observation
options.rationale: Egg allergy of any severity is not a contraindication to measles mumps rubella or influenza vaccine, both of which are given in general practice with the routine 15 minute observation period (Source: Australian Immunisation Handbook; ASCIA).

options.text: Arrange skin prick testing to each vaccine before administering it
options.rationale: Skin testing with vaccines has poor predictive value and is not recommended before routine immunisation of a child with food allergy (Source: ASCIA).

options.text: Give each vaccine in graded doses 30 minutes apart in the practice
options.rationale: Graded dosing is a specialist protocol used after a genuine vaccine reaction and has no role when the allergy is to a food rather than to a vaccine component (Source: ASCIA).

explanation.summary: Measles mumps rubella vaccine is grown in chick embryo fibroblast culture rather than in egg and contains no measurable ovalbumin, so egg allergy has never been a contraindication to it. Influenza vaccines are egg grown but modern manufacturing leaves ovalbumin content below 1 microgram per dose, a quantity well below any threshold for reaction, and large studies of children with egg anaphylaxis have shown no excess of reactions. Australian guidance is therefore that children with egg allergy of any severity, including anaphylaxis, receive both vaccines in the usual community setting with the standard 15 minute observation. The vaccine components that genuinely do warrant specialist assessment are gelatin and neomycin, and a previous anaphylactic reaction to a vaccine itself. Unnecessary referral is not neutral, because it delays immunisation and reinforces a family belief that vaccines are dangerous for their child.
key_points: Measles mumps rubella vaccine is not grown in egg and contains no ovalbumin
Influenza vaccines contain less than 1 microgram of ovalbumin per dose
Egg allergy of any severity is not a contraindication to either vaccine
Gelatin and neomycin allergy are the components that warrant specialist input
Unnecessary referral delays immunisation and reinforces vaccine anxiety
explanation.pearls: The one egg containing vaccine that still requires specialist assessment in Australia is yellow fever vaccine, which contains substantially more residual egg protein than influenza vaccine and is given under supervision in a designated travel clinic.

subtopic_detail: Applying low risk criteria to a transient event in a well infant
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 10 week old boy born at 39 weeks whose mother brought him in after an episode this afternoon. She says that while he was lying in his bouncer after a feed he went floppy and the skin around his lips turned blue for about 20 seconds, and that he came good when she picked him up and blew on his face.

Nobody gave rescue breaths or chest compressions. He has fed normally since and is now alert and interactive. He has had no fever, no cough and no vomiting, no similar episode before, and his immunisations are up to date. His examination including tone, fontanelle, femoral pulses and a full skin inspection is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 138 beats per minute, respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, blood pressure within normal limits for age
data_table.Examination: Alert and interactive, normal tone, soft fontanelle, symmetrical femoral pulses, no bruising or petechiae on full skin inspection, normal cardiovascular and respiratory examination
data_table.Observation: Four hours of cardiorespiratory monitoring in the emergency department with no further events

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for 24 hours of cardiorespiratory monitoring and observation
options.rationale: Prolonged monitoring does not improve outcomes in an infant meeting every low risk criterion and generates false alarms that lead to further unnecessary testing (Source: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram and a brain scan before discharge
options.rationale: Neurological investigation is indicated when the history describes focal features or when the examination is abnormal, and it has a very low yield after a single brief event with a normal examination (Source: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event

options.text: Perform a full septic screen including lumbar puncture and admit
options.rationale: A septic screen is driven by fever or an unwell appearance, and this afebrile well appearing infant with a normal examination does not meet the threshold (Source: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event

options.text: Educate the parents, offer resuscitation training and discharge
options.rationale: He meets every low risk criterion of age over 60 days, born at 32 weeks or later, a single event lasting under one minute, no cardiopulmonary resuscitation by a trained provider and a reassuring history and examination, so the recommended course is education, an offer of resuscitation training and discharge with follow up (Source: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event

options.text: Arrange a 24 hour oesophageal pH study and start a proton pump drug
options.rationale: Reflux is frequently assumed to be the cause of these events but pH studies do not establish causation, and acid suppression in infants carries risks of gastroenteritis and pneumonia without demonstrated benefit here (Source: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event

explanation.summary: The term brief resolved unexplained event replaced apparent life threatening event because the older label implied a danger that the evidence does not support, and it applies only when an infant under one year has a sudden brief episode of altered colour, tone, breathing or responsiveness that has fully resolved and has no explanation after history and examination. The value of the definition is that it creates an explicitly low risk group in whom extensive investigation and admission cause more harm than benefit. The criteria are age over 60 days, gestational age of 32 weeks or more with a corrected age of at least 45 weeks, a first event lasting less than one minute, no cardiopulmonary resuscitation by a trained provider, and a reassuring history and physical examination. Any infant failing a criterion is higher risk and needs individualised assessment, and the history should always include a careful and non accusatory consideration of inflicted injury, which is why a full skin inspection for bruising is part of the examination.
key_points: The event must have fully resolved and remain unexplained after history and examination
Low risk requires age over 60 days and a single event under one minute
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation by a trained provider excludes the low risk group
Extensive investigation in low risk infants causes net harm
Always inspect the skin for bruising and consider inflicted injury
explanation.pearls: An electrocardiogram is the one investigation reasonable to consider even in a low risk infant, because a long QT syndrome is otherwise undetectable on examination and is a treatable cause of sudden death.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Brief Resolved Unexplained Event
American Academy of Pediatrics Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: Sequencing treatment against imaging after an abnormal newborn screening result
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 7 day old girl recalled after her newborn screening card taken on day three flagged a raised thyroid stimulating hormone. Confirmatory venous blood taken this morning has just been reported.

She was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy, is breastfeeding slowly and sleeps through feeds. She is mildly jaundiced, has a large posterior fontanelle and mildly reduced tone, and no goitre is palpable. Her mother has no thyroid disease, has taken no antithyroid medication and has had no iodine containing contrast.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, respiratory rate 44 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 92 mIU/L (1-20 in the first week), free thyroxine 6 pmol/L (10-26), total bilirubin below the phototherapy threshold for age
data_table.Examination: Posterior fontanelle admitting a fingertip, mildly reduced tone, no goitre palpable, umbilicus healing normally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Await the thyroid scan result before starting any thyroid hormone
options.rationale: Every day of untreated hypothyroidism in the newborn period costs cognitive outcome, and imaging is not required to make the biochemical diagnosis (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism).

options.text: Repeat the venous thyroid function tests in two weeks and review
options.rationale: A repeat is appropriate for a borderline screening result with normal free thyroxine, and this infant already has unequivocal biochemical and clinical hypothyroidism (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism).

options.text: Commence thyroxine only if the thyroid scan shows no gland present
options.rationale: Treatment is determined by the biochemistry rather than the anatomy, since dyshormonogenesis with a normally sited gland causes hypothyroidism just as severe as agenesis (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism).

options.text: Refer to paediatric endocrinology for review within four weeks
options.rationale: Endocrine involvement is appropriate but a four week wait squanders the window in which treatment preserves cognitive outcome, which closes at around two weeks of age (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism).

options.text: Commence thyroxine today and arrange thyroid imaging in parallel
options.rationale: A markedly raised thyroid stimulating hormone with a low free thyroxine confirms congenital hypothyroidism, and thyroxine is started the same day while imaging to determine the underlying cause proceeds without delaying treatment (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Hypothyroidism; Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group).

explanation.summary: Congenital hypothyroidism affects about one in 2000 to 3000 births in Australia and is the commonest preventable cause of intellectual disability, which is why it has been part of newborn screening since the 1970s. Most affected infants have no clinical signs at birth because maternal thyroxine crosses the placenta, and the classic features of prolonged jaundice, a large posterior fontanelle, hypotonia, poor feeding, constipation and an umbilical hernia appear only as that supply is exhausted. Outcome depends almost entirely on how quickly treatment starts, with normal cognitive development expected when thyroxine begins within the first two weeks of life and a measurable loss of intelligence quotient for each week of delay thereafter. Imaging with ultrasound or a radionuclide scan distinguishes agenesis, an ectopic gland and dyshormonogenesis, which matters for genetic counselling and for deciding later whether a trial off treatment at three years is worthwhile, but it must never delay the first dose.
key_points: Most affected newborns appear normal because of transplacental maternal thyroxine
Treatment within the first two weeks of life preserves normal cognitive outcome
Imaging determines the cause but must not delay starting thyroxine
Dyshormonogenesis causes hypothyroidism as severe as glandular agenesis
Prolonged jaundice and a large posterior fontanelle are late clinical clues
explanation.pearls: The Australian starting dose is thyroxine 10 to 15 micrograms per kilogram daily, aiming to normalise the free thyroxine within two weeks, and the tablet is crushed in a small volume of water or breast milk rather than mixed into a full feed that the infant may not finish.
